Stammerers
STAM-ur-urz
n. pl. (those who stumble in speech; in Isaiah 32, they shall be ready to speak plainly)
From Old English stamerian, to stammer. At Isaiah 32:4 it renders Hebrew illeg, stuttering or stammering — used once in Scripture, in a promise about the coming reign of a King in righteousness.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 32 opens with a King who shall reign in righteousness, and the chapter describes His reign by what it repairs: And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken. The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. Four disabilities, and each is both physical and spiritual in the prophets' usage — dim eyes, deaf ears, a rash heart, a stumbling tongue. Under the King they are mended, and the last promise is given to men who could not get their words out: they shall speak plainly.

The Bible is unusually attentive to impediments of speech. Moses objected to his commission on exactly this ground — I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue — and was not excused but answered: Who hath made man's mouth? Isaiah elsewhere turns the image into judgment, saying that since the people would not hear plain Hebrew, with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people — the incomprehensible speech of an invading army. And Paul, who was accused at Corinth of being contemptible in speech, made the accusation into the argument: he came not with excellency of speech, so that their faith should not stand in the wisdom of men. The gospel has never depended on fluency, and Isaiah 32 promises that the men whose tongues fail them now will one day speak plainly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): those who stammer; persons who hesitate or stumble in speaking.

expand to see more

STAMMERER, n. One that stammers or hesitates in speaking.

STAMMER, v.i. To stop in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking.

ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.

PLAINLY, adv. In a plain manner; clearly; evidently; without disguise or ambiguity.

RASH, a. Hasty in counsel or action; precipitate; resolving or entering on a project without due deliberation.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 32:4 — "The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly."

Isaiah 32:3 — "And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken."

Exodus 4:10 — "And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue."

Isaiah 28:11 — "For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people."

Modern Corruption

Ministry is filtered by presentation, and the plain fact that God chose a man slow of speech to confront Pharaoh is preached but not practised.

expand to see more

The evangelical pulpit has been steadily conformed to the standards of the stage, and the men who rise in it are those who present well. Scripture's record runs strikingly the other way. Moses stammered and was sent anyway; Jeremiah said he could not speak, for he was a child; Paul was reckoned at Corinth to be weighty in his letters but weak in bodily presence and contemptible in speech, and answered by pointing out that the treasure is in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. A church that screens for fluency is screening on a criterion the Holy Ghost does not appear to use.

The promise of Isaiah 32 also deserves to be heard by those who carry a real impediment. The chapter is about a King reigning in righteousness, and one of the marks of His reign is that the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. That is not a demand made of them; it is something done for them. Until that day, the answer God gave Moses stands as the answer to every man who pleads his mouth as a reason to decline what he has been given: Who hath made man's mouth?... now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew illeg (H5926), stammering; laeg (H3934), of a foreign or mocking tongue; kebad peh (H3515 / H6310), heavy of mouth.

expand to see more

Hebrew illeg (H5926) — stammering; used once, in the promise of Isaiah 32:4.

Hebrew kebad peh (H3515, H6310) — heavy of mouth; Moses' description of himself at the bush.

Hebrew laeg (H3934) — stammering, foreign; the invading speech of Isaiah 28:11.

Hebrew tsachach (H6703) — clear, dazzling white; the root behind speak plainly.

Greek mogilalos (G3424) — having an impediment in speech; the man our Lord healed in Mark 7:32.

Usage

"“the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly” — a promise, not a demand."

"“I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” — the objection God overruled."

"“with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak” — the same image turned to judgment."
